capabilities.target: customer refund via payments processor (any order, up to order total)

inputs.source: Support staff request via SSO-authenticated channel

instructions.note: The agent may issue a refund for any order and any amount up to the order total based on its own judgment, with no per-staff cap, aggregate cap, or category restriction defined anywhere in the prompt.

'Use your judgment on partial refunds. Do not ask for confirmation.' makes the model's own judgment the only check on an irreversible financial action; no structural approval gate backs this decision.

controls.name: Refund amount capped at original order total
controls.decay_rationale: Enforced by the payments processor itself (a refund cannot exceed the order total), independent of model behavior. It narrows the maximum single-transaction loss but does not bound refund count, aggregate amount across orders, or require any human check, so it narrows rather than severs the path.

controls.name: Per-staff identity propagated to refund action and log (missing)
Adequate retention of staff refund requests (missing)

findings.title: Shared service account leaves refund actions unattributable and enables confused-deputy privilege (property finding)

forecast.watch_signal: The shared service account is extended to additional support tools, or any plan to propagate staff identity through to the processor log is dropped or deprioritized.

evidence.observation: The agent calls the payments processor with one shared service account used by every support tool, so the processor cannot distinguish which staff member initiated a given refund.
The processor log records the service account, the amount, and the order, but not which staff member asked or why.
The agent keeps no record of requests; staff chats are deleted after 7 days, removing the only other possible source of attribution.

recommendations.action: Replace the shared service account with per-staff delegated credentials or a signed identity token so each refund call to the payments processor carries the requesting staff member's identity.
Retain the staff request record (requester identity, order, amount, rationale) for an audit-adequate period instead of deleting chat logs after 7 days.

findings.title: No approval gate or aggregate spend/rate limit on irreversible refunds beyond the per-order cap (property finding)

forecast.watch_signal: The payments processor is configured to allow refunds exceeding the original order total (e.g., goodwill overrides), or the per-order cap is bypassed via repeated partial refund calls across orders.

evidence.observation: 'Use your judgment on partial refunds. Do not ask for confirmation.' removes any human check before an irreversible refund is issued; this instruction is part of the risk, not a control.
Refunds are irreversible once settled, usually within a day, so an erroneous or abusive refund cannot be undone after settlement.

recommendations.action: Require human approval with raw action review (full amount, order, and requester visible, not a collapsed summary) for refunds above a defined threshold.
Add a rolling per-staff and aggregate spend or count limit on refunds, independent of the per-order amount cap, to bound low-and-slow abuse.

stride_coverage.rationale: Artifacts do not describe protections against tampering with the agent's own configuration, prompt, or instructions.
Order data read is returned only to the requesting SSO-authenticated staff member who needs it to process the refund; no path to external disclosure is described.
Internal SSO-authenticated channel within the trust domain; this flow does not cross a trust boundary.
Internal SSO-authenticated channel within the trust domain; this flow does not cross a trust boundary.
Internal SSO-authenticated channel within the trust domain; this flow does not cross a trust boundary.
Artifacts do not describe transport integrity protections (e.g., TLS, request signing) for calls to the payments processor.
Data is sent to the payments processor, the intended and authorized recipient for issuing the refund; this is not disclosure to an unauthorized party.
Artifacts do not state whether the processor log is tamper-evident or append-only on the processor side.
Artifacts do not describe access controls on who may read the processor log.
The processor log is an external payment system record whose availability is outside this agent's design scope.
Artifacts do not describe integrity protections on staff chat history during its 7-day retention window.
Artifacts do not describe access controls on staff chat logs during their 7-day retention window.
This store is ephemeral chat history, not a component subject to denial-of-service concerns relevant to this assessment.
Artifacts do not state whether processor endpoint identity is verified (e.g., certificate pinning) before sending refund instructions.
The processor log is the record relied upon for repudiation of agent actions; the processor's own repudiation of receiving requests is outside this assessment's scope.

rating.rationale: No untrusted source reaches a sensitive sink today, so both findings are property findings (rubric 5a) rather than attack paths: a shared service account that strips staff attribution from every refund and payment read (repudiation and confused-deputy elevation of privilege), and the absence of any approval gate or aggregate spend/rate limit beyond the processor's built-in per-order cap, compounded by an explicit instruction not to seek confirmation. Both are capped at 'high' per the property-finding rule and driven to that tier by the autonomy modifier (no step or runtime limits are declared). The only credited control, the processor's per-order amount cap, is structural and independent but only narrows rather than severs the second finding's path, giving it a residual of 'moderate'; the attribution finding has no credited control at all and stays at 'high'. Forecast stays at 'high' overall because the attribution finding is already at the property-finding ceiling, though the spend-limit finding's own forecast rises from 'moderate' to 'high' if the per-order cap is weakened or bypassed (control_removal) or request volume grows (longer_task_horizon). The single control whose decay would matter most is ctl.order_cap_builtin, the per-order refund amount cap.

limitations: This assessment reflects the declared design and configuration described in the provided system prompt and runtime notes, not observed runtime behavior; actual agent behavior in production was not tested.

No MCP configuration, tool manifest, or IaC was provided; the payments processor integration, credential handling, and exact enforcement of the per-order cap are inferred from the runtime notes, so confidence on precise enforcement mechanisms is lower than it would be with verified configuration.

Whether SSO-authenticated staff identity is captured anywhere in the agent's own session state (even if not forwarded to the processor log or retained beyond 7 days) was not stated; if it is, the attribution gap may be partially mitigated outside the described chain and this assessment should be revised with that evidence.
